content: Pel-Ebstein fever is an uncommon clinical phenomenon observed in patients diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma. It is characterized by a cyclical pattern of fever, where the body temperature rises and falls over a period of approximately one to two weeks. This specific type of fever is also seen in other medical conditions, such as tuberculosis, but it is only referred to as Pel-Ebstein fever when it occurs in association with Hodgkin's lymphoma. The exact cause of Pel-Ebstein fever remains unknown. However, hypotheses suggest that it may be related to the host's immune response, necrosis of lymph nodes, or damage to stromal cells within the affected tissues. Management of Pel-Ebstein fever typically involves addressing the underlying Hodgkin's lymphoma, most commonly through chemotherapy. Symptomatic relief can also be achieved using nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The condition derives its name from Wilhelm Ebstein and P.K. Pel, who independently published descriptions of this phenomenon in 1887. There is ongoing debate within the medical community regarding the existence of Pel-Ebstein fever as a distinct clinical entity. In an article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, Richard Asher questioned whether the condition exists independently or merely because it has been given a name. He noted that it is widely recognized among medical students and physicians that cases of Hodgkin's disease may present with a fever that alternates between high and low phases on a weekly basis.
